## Learning Objectives

1. Analyze a single categorical variable using the \alert{binomial test}, a type of null hypothesis significance test
2. Determine when to use a binomial test
3. Estimate uncertainty of a proportion

## Pr[1 of 3 \alert{orange} M&Ms]

Using a \alert{probability tree} can help!

```{r, out.width = "75%"}

df_tree <- tibble(
  x = c(rep(0, 2), rep(2, 4), rep(4, 8)),
  y = c(rep(0, 2), rep(c(-2, 2), each = 2), rep(c(-3, -1, 1, 3), each = 2)),
  xend = x + 1,
  yend = c(-2, 2, -3, -1, 1, 3, -3.5, -2.5, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5)
)

df_label <- tibble(
  x = rep(c(1.5, 3.5, 5.5), c(2, 4, 8)),
  y = c(-2, 2, -3, -1, 1, 3, -3.5, -2.5, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5),
  color = rep(c("orange", "not orange"), 7),
  prob = rep(c("0.2", "0.8"), 7)
)

df_summary <- tidyr::crossing(
  prob1 = c(0.2, 0.8), prob2 = c(0.2, 0.8), prob3 = c(0.2, 0.8)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    x = 7,
    y = seq(-3.5, 3.5, 1),
    prob = glue("{prob1} %*% {prob2} %*% {prob3}")
  ) |>
  rowwise() |>
  summarize(
    x = x, y = y,
    prob = prob,
    n_orange = sum(c_across(matches("^prob[1-3]$")) == 0.2))

gp <- ggplot(df_tree, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
  xlim(-1, 8.5) + ylim(-4, 4) +
  geom_segment(size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(
    data = df_label,
    mapping = aes(x, y, fill = color), shape = 21,
    inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 6
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = df_label,
    mapping = aes(x - 1, y, label = prob),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 6
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = c(1.5, 3.5, 5.5), y= 4, label = str_c("M&M ", 1:3),
           size = 6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "orange")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size=10))) +
  # coord_equal() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.1, 0.9),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 18),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 18)
  )

gp
```

## Pr[1 of 3 \alert{orange} M&Ms]

Calculate probability of each outcome

```{r, out.width = "75%"}

gp + 
  geom_text(
    data = df_summary,
    mapping = aes(x, y, label = prob),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, parse = TRUE, size = 8
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 7, y= 4, label = "Probability", size = 6) 

```

## Pr[1 of 3 \alert{orange} M&Ms]

Count the ways to get desired outcome

```{r, out.width = "75%"}

gp + 
  geom_text(
    data = df_summary,
    mapping = aes(x, y, label = prob),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, parse = TRUE, size = 8
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 7, y= 4, label = "Probability", size = 6) +
  geom_text(
    data = df_summary,
    mapping = aes(x + 1.5, y, label = n_orange),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 8
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 8.5, y= 4, label = "italic(N)[orange]", size = 6, parse = TRUE) +
  NULL

```

## Pr[1 of 3 \alert{orange} M&Ms]

Add up probabilities: $3 \times (0.2 \times 0.8 \times 0.8) = `r dbinom(1, 3, 0.2)`$

```{r, out.width = "75%"}

gp + 
  geom_text(
    data = df_summary,
    mapping = aes(x, y, label = prob, color = n_orange == 1),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, parse = TRUE, size = 8, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("grey", "black")) +
  annotate("text", x = 7, y= 4, label = "Probability", size = 6) +
  geom_text(
    data = df_summary,
    mapping = aes(x + 1.5, y, label = n_orange, color = n_orange == 1),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 8, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 8.5, y= 4, label = "italic(N)[orange]", size = 6, parse = TRUE) +
  NULL

```

## Orange M&Ms

What is the probability of sampling 4 \alert{orange} M&Ms from a bag of 20 if $p = 0.2$ orange?

Drawing a probability tree would be too hard.

Fortunately, there's an equation!

## Binomial distribution

> The **binomial distribution** provides the probability distribution for the number of "successes" in a fixed number of independent trials, when the probability of success is the same in each trial.

Assumptions:

* the number of trials ($n$) is fixed
* separate trials are independent, and
* the probability of "success" ($p$) is the same in every trial

## Binomial distribution

$$\text{Pr}[X~\textit{successes}] = {n \choose X} p^X (1 - p)^{(n - X)}$$

- ${n \choose X}$: a count of the number of ways you could get $X$ successes in $n$ trials
- $p^X$: the probability of $X$ "successes" (multiplication rule)
- $(1-p)^{n-X}$: the probability of $n - X$ "failures" (multiplication rule)

## Binomial distribution (graphically)

$p \in {0.1, 0.5, 0.9}$

$n = 20$ trials

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

df <- tidyr::crossing(
  n = 20,
  `X successes` = 0:20,
  p = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)
) |>
  mutate(Probability = dbinom(`X successes`, n, p))

ggplot(df, aes(`X successes`, Probability)) +
  facet_grid(. ~ p, labeller = label_bquote(cols = italic(p) == .(p))) +
  geom_col(fill = "tomato") +
  theme_cowplot()

```

## Binomial distribution

What is the probability of sampling 4 \alert{orange} M&Ms from a bag of 20 if $p = 0.2$ orange?

General equation:

$$\text{Pr}[X~\textit{successes}] = {n \choose X} p^X (1 - p)^{(n - X)}$$
Equation for this example:

$$\text{Pr}[4~\alert{orange}~M\&Ms] = {20 \choose 4} 0.2^4 (1 - 0.2)^{(20 - 4)}$$

## Binomial distribution (graphically)

What is the probability of sampling $X$ \alert{orange} M&Ms from a bag of 20 if $p = 0.2$ orange?

$p = 0.2$

$n = 20$ trials

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, out.height = "50%", fig.width=4, fig.height=4, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

df <- tidyr::crossing(
  n = 20,
  `X successes` = 0:20,
  p = 0.2
) |>
  mutate(Probability = dbinom(`X successes`, n, p))

ggplot(df, aes(`X successes`, Probability)) +
  facet_grid(. ~ p, labeller = label_bquote(cols = italic(p) == .(p))) +
  geom_col(fill = "tomato") +
  xlab(expression(paste(italic(X), " orange M&Ms"))) +
  theme_cowplot()

```

## Summary

The \alert{binomial distribution} describes the probability of all possible outcomes from $n$ trials with probability of success $p$

Therefore, it is a \alert{sampling distribution} from a sample size of $n$ from a population where a proportion $p$ of the population is one discrete value (e.g. orange)

## M&Ms are fun and all... {.t}

But what are some biologically relevant examples?

## M&Ms are fun and all... {.t}

But what are some biologically relevant examples?

- Does a certain species prefer one habitat over another? \alert{test statistic:} number of occurrences in first habitat type versus the other
- Is a certain class of gene clustered on one chromosome? \alert{test statistic:} count of genes in the class on a specific chromosome versus all other chromosomes
- What is the dietary preference of some species? \alert{test statistic:} count of times the species ate one food type versus another

## \alert{Null Hypothesis Significance Testing}

1. State $H_0$ and $H_\mathrm{A}$
2. Calculate the test statistic
3. Generate the null distribution
4. Calculate the $P$-value
5. Decide:
    - Reject $H_0$ if $P$-value $\le \alpha$
    - Fail to reject $H_0$ if $P$-value $> \alpha$


## $H_0$ and $H_A$ deal with proportions

> A **proportion** is the fraction of individuals having a particular attribute.

$$p = \frac{\text{Number of "successes"}}{\text{Number of trials}}$$

Example: 21 out of 30 pulelehua Kamehameha caterpillars chose māmaki over *Urtica*, so the proportion is $\frac{21}{30}=0.7$

The **proportion** is a population parameter, and we can estimate it from data

## Parameter and estimate

 Parameter | Estimate
:---------:|:--------:
 $p$       | $\hat{p}$

## Food preferences of the pulelehua Kamehameha caterpiller {.t}

- $H_0$: The true population proportion $p = 0.5$
- $H_A$: The true population proportion $p \ne 0.5$
- Test statistic: (# times chose māmaki) = 21 out of 30
- What is the null distribution???

## Food preferences of the pulelehua Kamehameha caterpiller {.t}

- $H_0$: The true population proportion $p = 0.5$
- $H_A$: The true population proportion $p \ne 0.5$
- Test statistic: (# times chose māmaki) = 21 out of 30
- The null distribution is the \alert{binomial distribution} with $p = 0.5$

## Food preferences of the pulelehua Kamehameha caterpiller

\small
```{r echo = TRUE}
n <- 30 # number of trials

nsuccess <- 21 # number of times chose māmaki

p <- 0.5 # null hypothesis proportion

# P-value
upper <- pbinom(nsuccess, size = n, prob = p, 
                lower.tail = FALSE)
lower <- pbinom(n - nsuccess, size = n, prob = p, 
                lower.tail = TRUE)
pval <- upper + lower
pval
```

## Food preferences of the pulelehua Kamehameha caterpillar {.t}

- $H_0$: The true population proportion $p = 0.5$
- $H_A$: The true population proportion $p \ne 0.5$
- Test statistic: (# times chose māmaki) = 21 out of 30
- The null distribution is the \alert{binomial distribution} with $p = 0.5$
- With $P$-value = `r round(pval, 3)` we **reject** the null at $\alpha = 0.05$ significance


## Confidence Interval of a proportion {.t}

Remember, $\hat{p}$ (the proportion) is a sample estimate of the population parameter. Like any estimate we can calculate a confidence interval. But...
\vspace{2em}

The 2 SE rule does not work for 95% Confidence Intervals of the binomial distribution.


## Confidence Interval of a proportion {.t}

The 2 SE rule does not work for 95% Confidence Intervals of the binomial distribution. So...

We use R code instead

\small
```{r echo = TRUE}
n <- 30
nsuccess <- 21
phat <- nsuccess / n
phat

# 95% CI
ci95 <- qbinom(c(0.025, 0.975), n, phat) / n
ci95
```
